title: Nehemiah 9:1–8
context: On the twenty-fourth day of the same month the people assemble with fasting, sackcloth, and dust, separate themselves from foreigners, and confess their sins and the iniquities of their fathers, spending a fourth of the day reading the law and a fourth in confession and worship. Levites stand on the stairs and cry out, and then lead the people in a long prayer of praise and confession; the names in verses 4 and 5 differ from each other and from other Levite lists (compare Nehemiah 10:9; 12:8), and they are best read as given. The prayer begins with the LORD as the only God and maker of all things, who chose Abram, brought him from Ur, renamed him Abraham, found his heart faithful, and kept his covenant promise of the land because he is righteous. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about confession, God’s sovereignty in creation, and his faithfulness to his promises, while they describe differently how God’s choice of Abram relates to Abram’s faith.

verses.text: Now in the twenty-fourth day of this month the children of Israel were assembled with fasting, with sackcloth, and dirt on them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people assembling with fasting, sackcloth, and dust. Joy in the word is followed by sober repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the outward signs as expressing inward humility before God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a fitting response to the law’s conviction.

verses.text: The offspring of Israel separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people separating from foreigners and confessing their sins and their fathers’ iniquities. Repentance involves honest acknowledgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession as owning both personal and inherited guilt (compare Psalm 106:6). Both traditions commonly read the separation within its historical covenant setting, not as a rule against outsiders in general.

verses.text: They stood up in their place, and read in the book of the law of the LORD their God a fourth part of the day; and a fourth part they confessed and worshiped the LORD their God.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people reading the law for a quarter of the day and confessing and worshiping for another quarter. Word and response go together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pattern as Scripture leading to confession and praise. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of devotion shaped by God’s word.

verses.text: Then Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani of the Levites stood up on the stairs, and cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Levites standing on the stairs and crying out loudly to the LORD. Leaders give voice to the people’s prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levites leading the people in heartfelt prayer. Both traditions commonly read the names as given, noting that they differ from the list in the next verse.

verses.text: Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, “Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting! Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levites calling the people to stand and bless the LORD from everlasting to everlasting. Praise opens the confession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer beginning with God’s glory before turning to human sin. Readers in both traditions commonly hold up the verse as a model of starting prayer with worship.

verses.text: You are the LORD, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the confession that the LORD alone made heaven, earth, seas, and all their hosts, and preserves them all. God’s care sustains every creature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as affirming God’s sovereign creation and providence (compare Psalm 33:6; Colossians 1:17). Both traditions commonly read it as shared ground about God as Creator and Sustainer.

verses.text: You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram, brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees, gave him the name of Abraham,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD choosing Abram, bringing him from Ur, and renaming him Abraham. They commonly read God’s choice as a gracious calling to which Abram responded in faith (compare Hebrews 11:8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s choice of Abram as the free and sovereign beginning of the story (compare Genesis 11:31; 17:5). Readers in both traditions commonly agree that the choice was gracious and not earned.

verses.text: found his heart faithful before you, and made a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite, to give it to his offspring, and have performed your words, for you are righteous.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God finding Abraham’s heart faithful and making a covenant with him. They commonly read this as God recognizing genuine faith that responded to his call (compare Galatians 3:6).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Abraham’s faithful heart as the fruit of God’s gracious work in him. Both traditions commonly agree that God kept his promise because he is righteous.
